Introduction

Why Are We Here?

  • The Reality: Most computational research papers publish beautifully polished figures but hide the underlying source scripts.


  • The Excuses: “My code is too messy,” “Competitors will steal it,” or “I don’t have time to clean it up.”


  • Today’s Goal: We are going to stress-test these justifications using the arguments of Nick Barnes (2010) and Randall LeVeque (2013).

Overview: Barnes’ Paper

Most Software Isn’t Very Good

  • A Professional Perspective: Nick Barnes, a professional software engineer, shares a trade secret: most professional software inside consumer electronics is badly documented, inconsistent, and poorly tested.

  • The Scientist’s Assumption: Scientists generally withhold their code because they believe it is poor—lacking good comments, sensible variable names, or proper indentation.

  • The Reality Check: These formatting flaws do not matter to the core scientific record. Software across all trades is simply written to be good enough for the job intended.

What Happens to Science Software?

  • The Computational Reality: Turning raw laboratory data into published research papers inevitably requires programming and data manipulation.

  • The Patchwork Pipeline: Science code is often an awkward mix of small scripts to draw charts, larger filtering routines, and telemetry software glued together with piecemeal scripts.

  • The Disappearing History: While papers include a brief mathematical description of an algorithm, the actual software code usually languishes in an obscure folder or is simply deleted after publication.

Clean Enough vs. “Good Enough”

# The Real-World Research Script
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("temp_data_FIXED_FINAL_v2.csv") # Ugly hardcoded name!
res = [x * 4.219 for x in df['score'] if x > 0] # Messy magic number hack!
print("It works, leave it alone.")

  • The Psychological Barrier: Scientists frequently withhold code because they are embarrassed by non-standard syntax, messy comments, or unoptimized loops.

  • Ugly code is good enough: A dirty, functional script that exposes your actual workflow is infinitely superior to a hidden, “pristine” secret.

  • Not Commercial Software: Your code is an archive of an experiment, not an enterprise app. Readers do not expect commercial engineering standards—they expect scientific truth.

Openness Improves the Science

  • Case Study: NASA & Climate Code In 2007, NASA released its global temperature reporting software online. The code was messy and difficult for critics to run locally.

  • The Volunteer Audit: Volunteers rewrote the messy software to make it easier for non-experts to run. Through this open inspection, they discovered minor bugs.

  • The Ultimate Outcome: The bugs had zero bearing on the final scientific results, but NASA fixed them and ultimately chose to replace their original code with the volunteer version.

  • The Lesson: Science source code that is hidden from public scrutiny cannot benefit from peer review and rapid community improvements.

“No More Excuses” for Secrecy

  • “It is not common practice.”
    This is a cultural lag that must change across all fields.

  • “People will pick holes and demand support.”
    Not publishing code draws allegations of fraud, which is far worse. Furthermore, nobody is entitled to technical support for freely provided code; you can simply ignore unhelpful feedback.

  • “The code is valuable Intellectual Property.”
    Frankly, a little Python/R/Matlab routine is rarely worth money. Without ongoing backing by skilled experts, unshared institutional code just becomes un-useable “abandonware”.

Overcoming Computational Perfectionism

  • To scientists, the word “publication” signifies perfectionism.

  • This psychological wall stops researchers from releasing functional code because they feel it isn’t “polished” enough.

  • When publishing a paper, the original, raw script can simply be published as supplementary online information.

  • Ask yourself: Does your code perform the algorithm you describe in your paper? If it does, your audience will accept it “as is”. If it does not, you need to fix it anyway.

Overview: LeVeque’s Paper

The “Alternative Universe” Analogy

LeVeque asks us to imagine a world where mathematicians publish brilliant theorems but keep their proofs completely secret, expecting readers to simply “trust their reputation.”

In modern science, publishing a theorem without a proof is considered a joke.

Yet, publishing a computational figure without its source script is standard operating procedure.

The Hidden Value of Imperfect Scripts

  • Research Code vs. Enterprise Software
    Unlike commercial software, research code is not expected to be perfectly polished, but it is an essential part of the scientific record.

  • Code contains crucial details not present in the paper, serving as necessary documentation for the study.

  • Cleaning up code for public release is an effective way for researchers to uncover bugs in their own work.

What If You Cannot Share?

  • Partial Sharing: Even with proprietary restrictions, researchers can often share the specific, novel routines they developed for the paper.

  • Inspection Over Execution: Simply being able to read and inspect code is often more valuable to reviewers than running a compiled, black-box executable.

  • Alternative Mediums: If code cannot be shared digitally, publishing it as a static PDF appendix is a viable alternative.

The Self-Correction Effect

Almost every researcher who forces themselves to clean up and document their code for a public release uncovers hidden bugs, memory leaks, or flawed assumptions before publication.

  • The Blind Review Blindspot: Peer reviewers cannot catch internal logic flaws or scrambled data rows simply by staring at a static PDF chart or a final table of p-values.

  • Open Inspection over Execution: For many peer reviewers, simply being able to read the logic of the source text is vastly more informative than trying to run a compiled file.

  • The Crowdsourced Audit: Making your script open to the world allows outside domain experts to spot anomalies early, preventing high-profile retractions later on.

Transparency Maximizes Professional Impact

  • The Academic Currency: Code sharing is a major engine for professional discovery. Other scientists can only cite your work if they can easily adapt and extend your workflow.

  • Establishing Provenance: Publicly archiving your scripts on a hosted remote with a permanent DOI establishes clear, timestamped ownership over your unique algorithms.

  • Stopping Code Theft: If code sharing becomes standard operating procedure, it is significantly harder for competitors to secretly use your ideas without giving explicit citation credit.

  • Future Proof Competency: As the scientific community rapidly evolves, researchers who provide fully auditable pipelines are heavily favored by modern funding agencies and hiring committees.

Debate

02:00

Is a computer script fundamentally different from a mathematical proof, or are we just living in a scientifically immature era of computing?

Debate

🛡️ The Pragmatist View

It took me three years to write this algorithmic base. If I open-source it now, my competitors will use my code to publish five papers before I can even finish my next draft.

🌐 The Open View

Publicly archiving your code with a timestamped DOI is the absolute best way to claim ownership, establish provenance, and legally force competitors to cite you.

If you are a funding agency, how do you balance a scientist’s valid right to profit from their multi-year software labor against the public’s right to verify the data pipeline immediately?

04:00

Debate

Many researchers hide their scripts because they are terrified that once the code is public, their inbox will be flooded with emails from strangers asking for technical troubleshooting, custom modifications, or software installation help.

How do you draw a boundary between providing necessary scientific transparency and protecting your personal time from being hijacked by outside users demanding free tech support?

Poll

You are about to submit a paper. Your code works but is messy, uncommented, and unoptimized. What is your honest action?

  1. Publish it immediately: The dirty code is an essential part of the scientific record; transparency wins over aesthetics.

  2. Hide it entirely: I am too self-conscious about my coding skills; I would rather hide the script than face professional judgment.

  3. Delay the paper: Spend three weeks rewriting it neatly, even if it delays my graduation or submission timeline.

  4. The “Upon Request” Lie: State that the code is “available upon request” and hope no one ever actually emails me.

Poll

Why does the scientific community tolerate papers that publish computational figures but hide the source code scripts?

  1. Cultural Lag: Computing is relatively new to academia; we are simply living in a scientifically immature era of data science.

  2. Complexity: A computer script is infinitely more complex than a static math proof, making routine auditing impractical.

  3. Status Bias: We evaluate science based on the prestige and reputation of the author’s university rather than their code.

  4. Journal Laziness: Editors and peer reviewers simply refuse to force authors to change their habits because it adds extra work.

Final Words

Key Takeaways

  • Open science isn’t just an academic debate—it has high-stakes civic consequences.

  • Hidden code can carry direct life-or-death consequences in engineering and public policy.

  • Perfectionism and Absolute Secrecy both break scientific progress.

Key Takeaways

In the real world, engineering projects navigate this standoff through compromised structures:

  • The Production Sandbox: Tech firms can deposit source code into a Software Escrow—allowing a trusted, independent third-party academic panel to run line-by-line audits without exposing trade secrets to public competitors.

  • The Barnes Reality Check: Code does not need to be a beautifully polished product to be verified; it just needs to expose the raw mathematical parameters governing the bridge’s stress metrics.

  • The Baseline Rule: Un-auditable code is un-verifiable science.

The Selfish Benefits of Open Code

  • Your Most Important Collaborator: Your “past self” is your most frequent collaborator, and they notoriously forget what their own code did after 6 months.

  • The “Push-Button” Advantage: Forcing yourself to build a script that replicates your whole project with the push of a button pays off massively down the road.

  • Frictionless Revisions: When a journal reviewer inevitably demands you replot your data or shift an axis, an automated script saves you weeks of manual reconstruction labor.

  • The Institutional Shield: If your results are ever publicly questioned or audited by outsiders, a public, timestamped git repository provides immediate, undeniable proof of your data’s provenance.
